title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio

reading.body:
The core failure here is a training-data use question: an AI music generation system was built, allegedly, on copyrighted recordings whose rights holders had not authorized that use. The system then produced outputs that, according to the complaints, reproduced protected melodic and harmonic material closely enough to be identifiable. This is a deployment problem that originates at the data-curation stage, before any user ever types a prompt.

The litigation is multi-party and unresolved in important respects. Universal Music Group settled and reached a licensing arrangement with Udio. Warner Music Group did the same. Sony Music filed a separate lawsuit alleging approximately 30,000 recordings were used without authorization, and a judge declined to allow Sony to add that volume of recordings to its original case, prompting Sony to file a new, standalone suit. A class action brought by independent artists was not dismissed and was relocated from Illinois to New York. A musicians' union also filed suit over the UMG-Udio deal itself.

What is not established is whether any court has found Udio liable for copyright infringement, whether the alleged similarity of outputs to specific recordings constitutes infringement as a matter of law, or what the financial terms of any settlement are. The settlements resolve disputes between specific parties without producing findings of fact, and the remaining lawsuits are allegations, not verdicts.

summary:
Universal Music Group has settled a lawsuit against AI music startup Udio by reaching licensing agreements. The record label had accused Udio of using copyrighted songs to train its artificial intelligence system, which creates original music from text prompts. Under the settlement, Udio will launch a new platform next year that uses only authorized and licensed music, allowing users to customize, stream, and share songs. UMG's leadership stated the agreements reflect their commitment to supporting artists while embracing new technology and developing business models.

Udio, founded in 2024 by former Google DeepMind employees, declined to disclose the financial terms of the settlement. The company's AI had been accused of generating music similar to hits like The Temptations' "My Girl," reproducing the melody, chords, and backing vocals. Under the new arrangement, artists can opt into the platform and receive compensation, though specific details remain undisclosed. This marks Udio's first licensing agreement with a major music label.
